Introduction

Translation and Interpretation

Popol Wuj

by

Vincent James Stanzione

This is the Introduction to your reading of the Popol Wuj known in translation as the Book of Council of the Kʼicheʼ Maya of Guatemala. The Popol Wuj is the Kʼicheʼ Mayaʼs Sacred History that is the Ancestral Myth of the Kʼicheʼ People; Kʼicheʼ Pueblo. I have come to think of it as a Mythic History of Ancestral Writing original written a remembrance of ʼall that was done by the Kʼicheʼ People who lived and prospered as the Kʼicheʼ Pueblo who were, and continue to be, ʼMother-Fathers; Daughter-Sonsʼ of the Noble Territory known and named as Kʼicheʼ. This Book of Council; this Popol Wuj of the Noble Lords of Kʼicheʼ was once acted out and recited as the Ritual Drama that told the Ancestral History that was once danced and sung to form and shape the ways of Daughters and Sons in their initiatory transformation to be and become the ʼRefined Replacementsʼ and ʼDevoted Descendantsʼ of the Divine Ancestors of the Kʼicheʼ People; Kʼicheʼ Pueblo.

Guatemala the name that originates in the Nahuatl Cuauhtemallan or Place of the Many Trees known to the original People and Pueblo of Guatemala as: Kʼicheʼ. body: This Translation and Interpretation of the Popol Wuj will approach and address this Book of Council within the cultural context and natural world of the Kʼicheʼ People and their living as a Nation of Maya People that we will name the Kʼicheʼ Pueblo by following the way the Maya Scribes of the Kʼicheʼ Lineages who speak the Maya Kʼicheʼ language of the Kʼicheʼ People; Kʼicheʼ Winaq of the Kʼicheʼ Pueblo; Kʼicheʼ Amaqʼ. The Kʼicheʼ Pueblo; Kʼicheʼ Amaqʼ live in the noble realm and ancestral territory known as the Kʼicheʼ Kingdom; el Reino Kʼicheʼ; Rajawarem Kʼicheʼ so you as a reader know the nomenclature of these Maya People of the Forested Mountains of the Kʼicheʼ pronounces as: the English ʼkeyʼ and Cheʼ as in Cheʼ the Argentine naming of a friend; the name of Cheʼ Guevara to form the named “Key-Cheʼ” the Place of Many Trees; People of the Mountain Forest with many different varieties of Pines, Cypress, Oaks, Alders, Cherry, Elderberry, Corral Tree; Tzʼite, Avocado,  Willow, as well as the all important Reeds and Rushes that grow around its lakeshores. This translation will focus on this Natural World of the Kʼicheʼ with the Night Sky above reflecting the Sacred Landscape of the Face of the Earth below. This Interpretation is dedicated and devoted to the bringing forth the knowledge and remembrance of Kʼicheʼ Maya Ancestors who left their Ancient Ancestral Account as a ʼinstrument or toolʼ with which to ʼsee and knowʼ the Sacred Narrative of the Divine Ancestors and particularly the Hero Twins Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej and their story of change and transformation through their life and death ordeal in the Cave Realm where the Lords of Death test the ʼBoys, the Sons, the Twinsʼ in their Houses of Ordeal. All passages of the Popol Wuj are exciting to read once one understand how to read them but this section of the Popol Wuj that tells of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej is where we learn of the Twins and their Twinship ways that show the ʼancestral waysʼ of the Kʼicheʼ People. The Popol Wuj is about Twins and how to act and speak in collaborative and complementary ways of being and becoming in the world throughout a personʼs life. The Ancient Word;

body: Ojer Tzij of the Popol Wuj emphasize the balancing and harmonizing mutually beneficial ways in which the all beings live with one another on the Face of the Earth where everything and everybody are twinned with one another to be paired and coupled with one another in complementary ways. This is what I feel is the principal advice or counsel that the Popol Wuj leaves with us as ancestral wisdom and knowledge as to the way of living life. The Ancestral Couple are known as the Divine Ancestors who are the Grandmother; IxMuqane and Grandfather; Xpiyakok this Ancestral Pair are the Former, Shaper; the Creator, Crafter; the Molder, Modeler who are those who are named by their Ancient Animal Companion names in the Sacred Story of the Kʼicheʼ that is paired and coupled and twined as duos of complementary companions bring forth the world of the Maize Beings; Ixim Winaq who are the Kʼicheʼ Winaq; Kʼicheʼ Amaqʼ; the People, the Pueblo Kʼicheʼ. Great beauty sprouts forth from this harmony and balance of the Sky-Earth; Kaj-Ulew; Lake-Sea; Cho-Palo; Sun, Moon; Night, Day; Dark, Light; Tree, Vine; Mountain, Valley; Woman, Man that are best thought of complementary pairs that exist in a relationship of twinship with one-an-other. We often interpret this duality as coincidentia oppositorium that is often interpreted as two natural elements in contention with one-an-other instead of seeking the peace and harmony of warmth and light; wind and wetness to bring forth a flowering and fruiting world known as the Sky-Earth; Kaj-Ulew.

body: I remember how wonderful it made me feel when I first really understood this collaborative and complementary relationship with the Divine Ancestors; Mother-Father; Ancestral Couple; Ancient Pair forming and shaping the Sky-Earth with their thinking and contemplating with one another by celebrating council with one-an-other. And then I turned to the Hero Twins; Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej known in translation as One-Jun Blowgun Boy-AjPu to make the name One Blowgun Boy; One Hunter; and, his always super helpful savior of a brother: Little Jaguar-Deer; Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej; One Blowgun Boy and Little Jaguar Deer. These two brothers are perfect mirrored reflections of ʼone the otherʼ that collaborate and cooperate together, the two acting and speaking as one in completely collaborative and cooperative complementary companions. You get the idea with my exaggeration and emphasis of their relationship with one another as the cultural heroes that transform the Sky-Earth preparing it for the Ixim Winaq; the People of Maize. Junajpu and Ixbʼalamkej will transform into the Daytime Sun and Nighttime Sun as the Sun and Moon; the Moon who is known as the Little Hidden Jaguar Sun: Xbʼalankeʼ. The multiplicity of meanings of the names of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej brings us to a very important aspect of understanding and interpreting of the Popol Wuj which is it is a myth and because it is a myth there will never be any definitive translation and interpretations of its words and metaphors. They are always changing and transforming the more we understand the ways of the Ancient Maya and Mesoamerican People. We are in a period of recuperating the past that some very powerful people attempted to erase and eradicate. But the Ancient Mesoamerican past is constantly being brought forth through our continuous work interpreting all the art and architecture left by the Ancient Maya to immortalize themselves. The Maya wished to make themselves immortal through their painting and writing; carving and sculpture.

body:
This Translation and Interpretation of the Popol Wuj is my lifetimeʼs effort to bring the Popol Wuj a little closer to being understood within the context of the Kʼicheʼ Maya language and culture; religious practice and culture of the written word: sacred literature found here in the Popol Wuj that exists as a written manuscript . Let me explain a little bit about the manuscript protected in the Newberry Library in Chicago.

Because there so little time and space to tell the entire story of the Translation of the Popol Wuj let me present you with an orientation to what the Popol Wuj in the sense of a written document that is housed in a very special library. The copy of the Popol Wuj that exists today is a written document written out in ʼlong-handʼ by a Dominican Padre Francisco Ximénez.  Ximénez copy out the original Maya Kʼicheʼ writing written by the Kʼiche Maya Scribes of Noble Lineage who says we are writing out all that happened here in this place known as Kʼicheʼ. And this what they did, they wrote out their Ancestral History in the Latinate form that I will talk about below. The Dominican Padre Francisco Ximénez takes this document in Chichicastenango and copies it to then translate it into Spanish. It is a long story but this document known as Manuscrito de Chichicastenango leaves the Universidad de San Carlos the mid Nineteenth Century traveling to France and perhaps to Austria to then end up in England where it is collected by an American Collector Edward E. Ayer who in 1911 donated the Popol Wuj with another 17,000 documents to the Newberry Library of American Indian and Indigenous Studies.  The story of the Popol Wuj as ʼManuscriptʼ with a life of its own is a storybook tale in and of itself. So please suffice it to say that is it a miracle of sorts that the Popol Wuj exists for us to read today. I because of its precious nature I have devoted myself to assuring that its Translation and Interpretation are my best effort to bring for the good, the true, and the beautiful about the Popol Wuj through my philological studies of words and language and my ethnographic studies of culture, myth, and religion.

body: Approximately fifteen years ago I was working on a project at Harvard with Professor D. L. Carrasco who had invited me with many other scholars to collaborate in the interpretation of Ancient Indigenous ʼMapaʼ that told the ʼMythic Historyʼ of the People of Cuauhtinchan who illustrated and painted various Mapa de Cuauhtinchan. This highly capable group of scholars began teaching us in the group everything they knew and understood of the Mapa de Cuauhtinchan that we were invited to bring forth an Integral type Multi-Disciplinary type of interpretation that resulted in the book Cave, City, and Eagleʼs Nest: an Interpretive Journey through the Mapa de Cuauhtinchan Dos. The Mapa de Cuauhtinchan Dos is Mythic Mapa of Meaning for the Cuauhtinchan People who made-up the Pueblo of Cuauhtinchan which is to say that this group of erudite scholars agreed that it was through this Mapa that the Cuauhtinchantalaca expressed their ʼIdentityʼ through images and iconography that make-up the roads and places on the roads spoken about in a written document known as the Historia Tolteca-Chichimeca. I realized only after the publication of Cave, City, and Eagleʼs Nest that this was ʼthe seeing instrument; the seeing imageʼ to enliven oneʼs imagination in their desire to remember the ancestral past through the writing of words. This instrument for seeing is known as an ʼIlbʼalʼ and that is what the Pictorial Histories are in the context of the Mesoamerican World.

body: This knowledge and wisdom that patiently awaits our bringing it back into our consciousness as the Ancient Ancestral Ways of the Ancient Indigenous Ancestors who are very much alive in their descendants and replacement who are the millions of Maya speaking Maya living all over Southern Mexico in Vera Cruz, Campeche, Tabasco, Quintana Roo, Yucatan, Chiapas, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Belize, Canada, and now all over the United States of America. body:
Professor Patton began mentoring me and through her mentorship I began to realized my responsibility to the Kʼicheʼ Maya in specific and humanity in general which was to write a new translation and interpretation of the Popol Wuj. I came to realize through my work being edited by Professor Patton that since I could not recommend a translation that I knew was as good as it gets then it was up to me to bring out a translation of the Popol Wuj in English that reflected the Language and Culture; Myth and Religion of the Kʼicheʼ Maya. After all, I was the author of the “Junajpu and XBʼalamkiej The Hero Twins of the Popol Wuj” that I dedicated to the memory of my great hero of Mesoamerican Studies: Professor Alfredo López Austin. While writing that article on twins and twinship in the Popol Wuj I came to the conclusion that there were many good reasons to write this Translation and Interpretation of the Popol Wuj. And this is the result of that collaborative and complementary effort of working with scholars at the University of Harvard in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

The sacred stories found in Popol Wuj taken together provide all the counsel and advice the young women and young man could have ever asked for in their quest to become perfect replacements or replicas of their beloved ancestors; ancestors known to them as Nawal Winaq: Magical Transforming Ancestors. These Divine Ancestors were capable of magical transformation that enabled them to become whatever was necessary to bring about change and transformation in the World known as the Sky-Earth, Kaj-Ulew. Popol Wuj tells us of these Nawal Winaq while providing their descendants counsel through sacred story or myth in order that they survive rites of initiation in order to then thrive on the path of their becoming Divine Ancestors by repeating their ancestral speech and exemplary actions.

body:
It was through experiencing the sacred stories here that members of the Kʼicheʼ community would then participate in their being sung and danced, played and performed during the New Years Ceremonies that took place at the pivot of the years between the dry and rainy season when maize was sown and the New Year was borne into time through the ritual of sacrifice experienced as the waiting for the dawn at the ʼComing out place of the Sunʼ that took place upon mountain tops all across the Mesoamerican World. Popol Wuj is the sacred story that informed this ritual of renewal that was also a rite of initiation. Popol Wuj tells of the obstacles found on the path of becoming an adult member of the Kʼicheʼ People as well as how to overcome the rivals, adversaries, and enemies that one eventually encounters in life. Life is a continual test of oneʼs abilities to overcome adversity in order to rise up like the sun to shine oneʼs light on all that seeks warmth to grow. This light and warmth of the Sun that is brought forth throughout the many stories told throughout the Popol Wuj with its many changing and transforming narratives.  Popol Wuj is truly the Book of Council from which everyone of any age can gain greater understanding and advice in the human struggle of life.

My relationship goes back forty years when I first read it in a class on Spanish American Literature where we learned that the Popol Wuj was the work of Dominican Friar Francisco Ximénez when in fact the Maya Scribes of Popol Wuj name themselves as the Nim Chʼokoj Ajaw, the Scribal Lords of the Great Mico de León lineages of the Kaweq, Nijaʼibʼ and Ajaw Kʼicheʼ. They named their names saying they were the Mother-Fathers of the Word and Masters of the Ritual Performance of the Dances that told the stories found in Popol Wuj. Perhaps these Mother-Fathers of the Ancestral Word were even the narrators of the ritual drama of Popol Wuj presented at the New Year; ritual drama that renewed the Kʼicheʼ world and lives of the Kʼicheʼ People.

body:
In my lifetime so much has changed with regard to the Popol Wuj: the way we now decolonize its colonial orthography, our deep understanding of myth and humanityʼs need of mythic narratives, our knowledge of the Maya Kʼicheʼ language in order to translated it with insight and erudition, and, in my case, after living with the Maya for the last thirty-five years, our generation has been enabled by human ethics and compassion we have become a much more diverse people capable of integrating the ʼintimate otherʼ into our hearts and souls. It has been this move to ʼdecolonizeʼ myself that has allowed me to translate this ancient myth of the Maya into a poetic form of English that does not betray the original mythic language that Maya scribes wrote this Book of Council known as Popol Wuj.

The Nim Chʼokoj Ajaw based their Latinate rendition of this ancient, ancient story of the “the sowing and dawning of life for peopling of the face of the earth” on a hieroglyphic or epigraphic text in their own Maya Kʼicheʼ language. This hieroglyphic text is mentioned by the Nim Chokoj Ajaw as the Popol Wuj. Today the Kʼicheʼ Maya of Chichicastenango want everyone to know that their Popol Wuj did not begin with the copying and translation of Ximénez but with Kʼicheʼ Maya scribes who wrote it between the years of 1554-1558.. These women and men scribes are Masters of Ceremony thus they are Masters of the Ancient Word, Ancient Traditions. So they donʼt invent the Popol Wuj as an act of inspired artistic creation. These scribes were well educated in the art of the ancestral word, which is grounded in the ancestral art of memory guided by a written text sung as an incantation of the Ancient World or Sky-Earth that was literally danced into life.

body:
We know that Francisco Ximénez studies the Popol Wuj in We know that Francisco Ximénez studies the Popol Wuj in the years of 1701-1703 right here in Chichicastenango when and where he makes a perfect copy of it to work on later in the Kʼicheʼ Maya town of Rabinal when he finds enough time to carry on such an arduous scholarly task. What is most infuriating for Maya Activist and Day-keepers about the work of Ximénez is his calling the Popol Wuj the work of Lucifer and that it is full of lies formulated by Satanas. These words have never been properly addressed by Catholic Authorities and because of that there remains an ambiguous acceptance of this great hero of the Popol Wuj who literally saved it from extinction. This is an aspect of the Popol Wuj and its connection with the Dominican Order that is just another irony of the many ironies of the Spanish Empire and its many agents of the Crown and Church in the New World.

It isnʼt until 1857 that Carl Scherzer, an Austrian physician following up on the advice of Prussian naturalist Alexander von Humboldt, published the Spanish translation of Ximénez after he passes through Mexico at the end of his travels in the New World, Von Humboldt encouraged many Europeans to study Mesoamerican people.

In 1861, Charles Etienne Brasseur de Bourbourg in Paris works to translate the Popol Wuj into French while publishing the Maya Kʼicheʼ text copied by Ximénez at the same time, after all he was in possession of the original copy at this time. In 1911, after moving from one place to another in Europe, the Popol Wuj ended up safely at the Newberry Library in Chicago where it lives on today. But the translation of the Popol Wuj does not end there, not at all.

In 1944, Leonhard S. Schultze Jena published a German translation titled Popol Vuh: Das heilege Buch der Quiche-Indianer von Guatemala in Stuttgart.

In 1947, Kʼicheʼ Maya translator and scholar Adrián Recinos published an edition in Spanish titled Popol-Vuh: Las Antiguas Historias de Quiche, which was republished by el Fondo de Cultura Económico in 1953.

body:
This translation of the Popol Wuj by Recinos is retranslated into English in 1950. Entitled Popol Vuh: the Sacred Book of the Quiche ʼ Maya of Guatemala, it featured a new introduction by educator Delia Goetz and archaeologist Sylvanus Griswold Morley.

In 1965 José Antonio Villacorta published a fascinating volume title El Popol-Vuj en Crestomatía quiche in which a Spanish translation is translated word by word beneath the original Maya Kʼicheʼ text of Ximénez. This bilingual edition is twinned with a second volume in Spanish that provides an exegesis of the Popol Wuj narrative complete with ideas from the times.

Then in New Orleans, at Tulane University, Munro Edmonson published two remarkable editions that would change the translation of the Popol Wuj forever more. In 1965 Edmonson publishes the Quiche-English Dictionary, an all-encompassing dictionary that laid the ground work for Edmonsonʼs 1971 masterpiece of translation titled The Book of Counsel: The Popol Vuj of the Quiche Maya of Guatemala.

In 1973 Agustín Estrada Monroy published is Spanish facsimile edition titled Popol Vuj which came out after the Popol Wuj was made the Libro Nacional de Guatemala in 1971. This was an attempt by the dominant culture to take control of this Maya narrative that was seen by most people as an attempt to steal the fire from the Kʼicheʼ Maya by colonizing the very work that would have given the Kʼicheʼ Maya an opportunity to present their Ancient Word in their own way.

But before Luis Enrique Sam Colop published his work, another scholar of Native American and Mesoamerican Language and Literature, Dennis Tedlock (a student of Edmonson), in 1985, published Popol Vuh: The Definitive Edition of the Mayan Book of the Dawn of Life and the Glories of Gods and Kings. Tedlock sold bountiful copies of his Popol Wuj that many consider more an imaginative flight into the realm known as poetic license, setting the stage for ever more ʼimaginativeʼ translations to come.

In 1998 Luis Enrique Sam Colop published his Popol Wuj: Versión Poética Kʼicheʼ alongside a twinned Spanish edition, each language mirroring the other in precise ways. Colop was a student of Tedlock who was a student of Edmonson who was a student of Clyde Kluckhohn of Harvard University. The work of Sam Colop is excellent yet he does make some mistakes with regard to nature that are difficult to understand.

Allen J. Christensonʼs translation, Popol Vuj: Sacred Book of the Maya: the Great Classic of Central American Spirituality, translated from the Original Maya text.  This is the hardest working and most dedicated Translator to have ever worked in the field of Mesoamerican Studies alongside his colleagues Robert Carmack and James Mondloch. This authorʼs dedication to the Maya is nothing less than exemplary and one often has the feeling as if he were of Maya descent himself because of the way he connects with the Maya Culture and Civilization.

In 2018 linguist James Mondloch and anthropologist Robert Carmack published a Spanish-Maya Kʼicheʼ translation, Popol Wuj: Nueva Traducción y Comentarios (Publicaciones Mesoamericanas) with the original text of none other than Padre Francisco Ximénez. I find this work to be a true masterpiece of scholarly rigor, scope, and design; a true monument to a lifetime of dedication to the Kʼicheʼ Maya by both of this extraordinary Maya Scholars. This masterwork of Carmack and Mondloch is the most beneficial translation in existence today, making it an extremely important document for the many translations that will come forth in the future of the Popol Wuj.

Humberto Akʼabʼal and his edition of the Popol Wuj that is not a translation in the strictest sense of the word and this is precisely why I have not been able to include the beautiful poetic work of Humberto Akʼabʼal as a Translation. But I would like to mention the storytelling version of the Humberto Akʼabʼal and his Popol Wuj because his poetry and lifetime struggle as an Maya Activist and Poet has influenced my translation of the Popol Wuj in poetic ways..

body:
So why have I taken up the honorable task of translating the Popol Wuj as a student of Professor David L. Carrasco and Professor Emeritus C. H. Long from the University of the Chicagoʼs authoritative lineage of Historians of Religion?  The answer is quite simple: none of the previous translations take seriously the art of interpretation known as hermeneutics. Nor do they take seriously the truth that language is sacred speech and must be treated as the sacred speech of Divine Ancestors who are understood to be the formers and shapers of the Ancient Word, Ojer Tzij that the academic tradition calls sacred history or myth. None of the previous translations opened up and entered their interpretation and interpretive understanding of the Maya Kʼicheʼ text through the hermeneutical perspective as a historian of religion.

Nor have past translators of English been able to call upon over three decades of human experience living, laughing, flying, joking, working, walking, watching, waiting, standing, sitting, singing, studying, teaching, typing, dancing, playing, praying, speaking, guiding, buying, selling, building, cutting, carving, chopping, sowing, seeding, sighing, loving, laughing, crying, researching, and writing right alongside the Maya of thee Highlands, Lowlands, and Boca Costa of Guatemala.  I really actually live in the countryside out in the mountains of the Western Highlands; out in the woods in the forest of what is known en la montaña or up in the mountains.

My life lived with Maya Kʼicheʼ, Kaqchikel, and Tzʼutujil speaking Maya people has provided me with a very profound human perspective that has enabled me to approach this sacred Maya history in a very down to earth, existentialist way. I cherish this perspective that has developed in me through very natural, human ways. None of the other translators seemed to study this Maya myth as serio ludare, serious play, as James Hillman taught me to say. For the Popol Wuj is the Mayaʼs expression of soul whose recitation and performance of the story through metaphorical words and archetypal actions bring out the ancestors spiritual and physical presences into the present day.

body:
As the historian of religions Mircea Eliade understood and expressed throughout his writing, myth records the divine actions and creations of deities and revered ancestors that are continually told and retold through the repetition of mythic archetypes that are imitated and performed for the renovation and renewal of community. Myth as the Popol Wuj says over and over forms and shapes the community by forming and shaping the people with its metaphors of being and becoming that are the actions of the artists and artisans of making and modeling and molding to form and shape the world around one so that world in turn forms and shapes one through metaphor of myth which is the Former and Shaper forming and shaping the World and all of its beings the human beings much included as being formed and shaped from maize.

Eliadeʼs colleague at the University of Chicago, Charles H. Long, in his classic text Alpha: The Myths of Creation, revealed the deepest understanding of myth which is that the repetitive yearly recitation or performance of myths of creation that brings forth the sowing and sprouting of maize and the dawning of a New Yearʼs sun imitate the renewal of the human soul as it is transformed through ordeals of initiation through the underworld.

Carrascoʼs work on the Quetzalcoatl, the Plumed Serpent or Qʼuqʼkumatz, Kukulkan of the Maya and Mexica traditions has shown how creation myths performed through ritual drama are the communities experience revitalization in sacred precincts, communal places, and community identity. Carrascoʼs work on Quetzalcoatl awakens one to the understanding that Popol Wuj is a Mesoamerican narrative as Lord Nakxitl becomes the very pivot of the Four Quarters of the Nahua Empire of centered in the Tollan Tzuy-Wa at the Coming Out Place of the Sun. What most people do not understand about the Popol Wuj is that the after the Forming and Shaping of the First Four Fathers of the Kʼicheʼ the Sacred History of Mesoamerican People begins when they decide that if they want to have guidance and protection in their lives they will need a Deity known as a Kabʼawil to guide and protect them.

body: This is where my work on Quetzalcoatl with Carrasco forty years ago sings out as a remembrance of my own need to return to my origins as the First Four Fathers will ask their Sons; Grandsons to remember them by returning to their origins at the Coming Out Place of the Sun at Tollan Tzuy-Wa.  This is why the Popol Wuj is so fascinating because it has the capacity for oneʼs life to become enveloped in its sacred narrative so that we realize the archetypes demand repetition. And so it is my joy translating the Popol Wuj to be writing about Lord Quetzalcoatl as Great Lord of the People of the Coming Out Place of the Sun. And so through the Popol Wuj I have been able to return to this powerful understanding of Lord Quetzalcoatl at the Center of the Mesoamerican Word on his Reed Mat Jaguar Throne waiting for the Sons of the First Four Fathers to arrive to receive their emblems of investiture as well as their signs and symbols of power and authority to rule and govern the Kʼicheʼ Kingdom as the Replacements of their Divine Ancestors. Carrascoʼs interpretive teaching taught me the hermeneutic technique that has enabled me to work through the Interpretive Commentary as Hermeneutic in which the Culture Horizons from the world I came from become fused with the Cultural Horizons of the Mesoamerican World that is the Maya World so that I am able to open my reader to a New World that is the Indigenous World of the Kʼicheʼ Maya People; Kʼicheʼ Maya Pueblo. And to be honest this is only through the teaching of Professor Charles H. Long and Professor Davíd L. Carrasco that I ever learned this Art and Science of Interpretation that is Hermeneutics.

body: Along with Eliadeʼs profound insights into humanityʼs quest for the eternal return through rites of initiation, as well as his work in comparative religion regarding the vital powers and archaic patterns in nature and the cosmos that orient and shape human consciousness I have been able to understand the rites of initiation experienced throughout the Popol Wuj. Eliadeʼs work on Rites of Initiation focus oneʼs understanding of the trials, tests, and ordeals in the House of Xibʼalbʼa that the Hero Twins must survive during the Night to then be made to play ball at Dawn at the sunʼs first light. This pattern of initiation is only suggested in the Popol Wuj. Nowhere are we told this is the pattern of Maya Religion that the Youth from the Youth Houses were made to suffer to survive. But we know it is there in the Popol Wuj for the Kʼicheʼ Maya Youth who want to become the Ball-players and Warriors must face death in the Six Houses of Xibʼalbʼa: Dark House; Cold House; Jaguar House; Fire House; Obsidian Blade House and Killer Bat House. Eliadeʼs ideas provided an interpretive framework through which I was able to begin interpreting in order to eventual translate the Popol Wuj and its ʼsecretʼ sacred language with which its scribes brought it forth into existence as a Maya Kʼicheʼ text.

body:
My strengths as a translator are founded in what my teachers taught me long ago. Carrasco and Long provided me with everything I needed to know in order to live in the ʼfieldʼ I would write about ever since my cultural, psychological, and physical departure from the Mesoamerican Archive and Research Project. I stayed very connect to Professors Long and Carrasco, my notebooks of notes I took on their classes and books are right here on my table as I write this as talisman of sorts that I bear with me as sacred symbols of power and authority to interpret sacred language and mythological text. These men as my teachers are on my mind constantly all these decades latter not because I didnʼt keep reading other writers and authors in say Archetypal Psychology or Maya studies in specific but the truth be told my teachers were and are my teachers and that is the way a Traditionalist like myself lives his lives. I can, and have read, Long, Carrasco, and Eliade over and over through the years and there it is; their teaching rings true. And so you shall see with the Interpretations of the Popol Wuj. If you know their work you will hear it in mine.

Yes, I did need to ʼchange placeʼ after thirty years of living out of place as Latinate Italian-America searching for an Indigenous American identity that was always easy for me to find because of my ease with people in the countryside and my enjoyment of being just part of the Pueblo. Yes, I was called to a new sacred landscape where the Maya were living in their world as a strong, empowered yet oppressed majority whose voice had been silenced by death as mine has been silenced still. I donʼt say what I really think of these other translation or translators. That is no way to act in a world that says, if you canʼt say something nice then donʼt say anything at all. But I would like to say what I think of some of these translations and translators who have obviously conquered to colonize the Popol Wuj for their own well being. But the Maya taught me never say a word, never let the enemy know that you are at war, donʼt say a word; donʼt let them know, never.

body:
By learning to speak Maya languages I would find another world within my kernel of being that would sprout forth from the dark underworld of my lifeʼs own sort of repression to rise-up and out anew like the green maize shoot come back to life to climb like a strong green cane reaching for the Heart of the Sky. I sought out the indigenous voice that was watching and waiting for the dawn in order to rise up like the sun, bright and bold, clear and crisp, renewed after living so long in the underworld of my own terrible fear and confusion as a lone gringo out in the forest with his strong, determined artists-artisan woman companion more than even a wife a complement and empowerment in life.

My teachers provided me with an intellectual inheritance that taught me how to read and interpret myth as the sacred history of another while instructing me on how to interpret a text by asking questions that attempted to eliminate the distance between myself and the beloved and respected other as another human soul. It was up to me to find the words to say it and I would find them time and again. In fact I would find a lot of words and I would say them by writing a book titled Rituals of Sacrifice: Walking the Face of the Earth on the Sacred Path of the Sun. It was in that book I would recognize my debt to Carrasco, Eliade, and Long while Long and Carrasco recognized my debt to them and their special school and style of teaching hermeneutics in the discipline known as the History of Religion. You need to know this because you need to know that this translation and interpretation is a translation and interpretation that has taken the form and shape of a Historian of Religion who was an eternal student of myth and myths eternal return in the mythic tradition of Mesoamerica.

body:
By studying myth once again as the expression of the human soul I discovered a way back to the creative yet grounded work of those archetypal psychologists who worked with historians of religion as humanists at places like Eranos.  None of the other translators seem to understand what religious historian Mircea Eliade wrote about so well, which is that the sacred literature we call myth is an expression of the experience of the human soul as it transforms through ordeal in its journey through the underworld.

Mircea Eliadeʼs profound insights into humanityʼs quest of the eternal return through rites of initiation continue to be the best orientation to an interpretive reading and interpretation of the Popol Wuj. Mircea Eliadeʼs work in Comparative Religion guides the translator down the path of understanding the secret sacred language used to throughout the Popol Wuj. Eliade and Long were gifted thinkers and translators of sacred words in their own right but it was my teacher David L. Carrasco that taught me how to interpret mythos as divine expressions brought forth by human beings.

It was the way Carrasco ʼentered the wordʼ whenever he offered an interpretation of the text by first asking the question of who wrote this text, when and where and why all in order to understand the context within which the text had been written in order to better understand the words that formed the metaphors that shaped the myth or mythic literature we were studying. Carrasco was always about giving space so one could understand how an author had taken the center most place to create meaning from words that were placed together just so the create a particular meaning. This understanding of particular meanings is the work of a translator who moves back and forth from a particular context to a general context; from a part to a whole. It is this back and forth play of translation that eventually leads one to finding the most profound understanding and insight about a particular word or phrase.

body:
But I suspect it was Long, Eliade, and James Hillman along with Carrasco who taught me about the soul of words and the soulful metaphors heard beating in soul of the Ancient Word, Ojer Tzij. This heart beat of soul reverberating as palpitation of mythic world with its mythic figures, mythic archetypes that came to life through ones capacity to give oneself complete to the experience of entering the word. This divine human act of allowing a text to palpate in the very center, in the very heart and soul with the express desire to transform oneʼs perspective of life and oneʼs purpose in life lived out in this world. Past translation simple lacked this deep love for the ancestral soul of the Ancient Word of the Maya. Yes, it was a matter of aesthetics but it was more a matter of love, love for a people who I seemed to know the moment I sat down with them on a long wooden bench listening to perfection of their ancient, ancestral word.

Love of the other, oneʼs self, and the world goes a long way to answering why I translated the Popol Wuj for the coming generations of Maya-Americans and Mexican-Americans for whom I have worked so diligently. My teachers werenʼt in the game to rise up above all the rest at any cost. No, my teachers were, and continue to be activist, who called me towards a higher more humanitarian goal. This is why I chose to translate through the thought of the heart in order to interpret the Maya myth of the Popol Wuj for the descendants of those who wrote so very, very long ago.

A translator must enter the language they are translating not as a linguist who is interested in words as separate parts of a whole, but as a historian of religion who understands that sacred words must be comprehended as living beings which animate relationships as a greater whole known as an Indigenous People, a Native America Pueblo who see themselves as the Divine Descendants of Divine Ancestors. The Popol Wuj in my translation is understood as the very heart and soul of the Kʼicheʼ Maya of the Maya Kʼiche speaking and writing Pueblo of Kʼicheʼ People.

body:
There is both terror and luck to be found in history. We should feel lucky that we can speak with Kʼicheʼ Maya of Highland and Lowland Guatemala in the same Maya Kʼicheʼ language their sacred history, the Popol Wuj, was written.

The Maya have taught me that one must know their land with its light, shadow, and darknesses; one must understand nature and its ways; one must feel their words as thought of the heart; and, perhaps most of all sense the beauty that touches oneʼs soul. These lessons shaped how I translated and interpreted the Popol Wuj while knowing there is never a possibility of creating a literal translation because every word, written or spoken, is a metaphor for a meaning we must experience in order to feel our way through the living pathways of the word that is myth; a myth that is a sacred story that speaks to our human soul.

By coming to know this myth as a manifestation of Maya language as it names the ancestral beings and their sacred spaces that create the mythic landscape we move through as we become the actors in this serious play known as the Popol Wuj. By becoming a bit more Mayan we truly become a bit more American, but American in the most integrated sense of that name, of that word; American in the hemispheric sense of what that word, that name, meant five centuries ago. To be American must eventually come to mean knowing a Native American language so let us begin to transform our transient sense of self through the sacred words of the many names and places found in the Popol Wuj.

body:
I say this because I know for certain that the Popol Wuj is Ancient Americaʼs greatest masterpiece of Native American mythological writing, there is nothing else quite like it. This is why I wanted to translate it into English in indigenous ways; ways that feed our indigenous American soul. Ways in which Judeo-Christian and Greco-Roman influences are expunged from the Mayaʼs Ancient Word-Ojer Tzij in order that the indigenous soul of the America is heard, loud and clear. In this way our understanding and interpretation of Popol Wuj mirrors the experience of its performance by the Kʼiche Mayaʼs experience of their own Maya Kʼicheʼ language, thus the soul of the Maya is experienced by us, those who which to comprehend the Popol Wuj as an experience of the human soul.

In this since my translation is more a reflection of Maya experience of their humor and imagination as sustenance of the human soul. This rich vein of humor and deep sense of imagination reveal themselves in the imaginal world formed and fashioned through Maya poetics with its multifarious word-play and multiple meaning metaphors that manifest the mythological magic of this exquisite ancestral incantation of this hemisphereʼs original mythos: Americaʼs most authentic indigenous word.

The Nim Chʼokoj Ajaw were not only scribes, they were not only Mother-Fathers of the Word, for they were also ceremonial specialist who organized the ritual performance and sacred recitation of the Popol Wuj. It was through their direction of song and dance that the voice and movement of the Heart of the Sky, Heart of the Earth was expressed as the heartfelt experience of the Maya Soul. It was through the direction and guidance of these ceremonial specialist known as Nim Chʼokoj Ajaw that the ancestral ways of the Divine Couple, Divine Pair was brought out to guide and protect their descendants every step of the way as their ancestral soul made its journey through the original Maya Kʼicheʼ version of the Popol Wuj.

body: We know the Popol Wuj has been with the Mesoamerican culture and language for as long as Mesoamericans have been created painted ceramics, stone carvings, wood statuary, clay figurines, and hieroglyphic storybooks. We know this because the archetypal images and mythic figures of the Popol Wuj have spoken to us across time. The presence of this Mesoamerican-Maya myth is what has formed and shaped the art and architecture of the Maya-Mesoamerica from the first images this human tradition made and modeled, carved and sculpted, drew and painted since time immemorial. And there at heart of this mythic tradition is the center place where the Heart of the Sky, Heart of the Earth; Ukʼux Kaj, Ukʼux Ulew stand as the pillar at the very pivot of the Four Quarters. It is their primordial power as pillar and pivot that ancestral energies of center and periphery gather together in order to spin to the left as the movement of song and dance that are the essence of the Mayaʼs poetic sense of soul.

body: This is the sacred story the Kʼicheʼ Mayaʼs Popol Wuj tells us as it shows us the way of life and death by entering into the sacred word of myth. It is through the Mayaʼs refined sense of mythic language that the ecstatic movement of song and dance brings forth essential nature and understanding of life and death, heaven and earth, men and women, fire and water, sun and moon, eagle and jaguar, the blue and the red, body and blood, maize and cacao, spinning and weaving, knotting and loosening, above and below, light and dark, daughter and son, mother and father, ancient and renewed, hunter and hunted, grown and gathered, sown and sprouted, on and off goes the endless movement of the nuclear cores, the essential hearts, the hard kernels of Mesoamerican culture and religion that are revealed throughout the Popol Wuj; all of which I wished as I hoped as I worked in ecstasy and struggled through pain to bring this magnificent Mesoamerican-Maya world to life in English. This is why I wanted to translate the Popol Wuj and because of this hunger to bring out the mythic soul through the mythic essence of the Popol Wuj enabling me to do what I had to do, did what I did to have done what I have done by following the mythic way of the Ancient Word: Ojer Tzij known as the Ancestral Fire, Ancient Tradition, Old Ways, Ancestral Story; Popol Wuj, the Book of Council by any other name

body: This then is the Sacred History of Ancestral Realm of the Kʼicheʼ with its continuously transforming and developing Ages; the Sun; the Eras that transform into the Generations of the Kʼicheʼ Lineages of the Kʼicheʼ Kingdom and their transformation from beginning to end with the Kʼicheʼ Nobles concluding their rulership with the last words of the Popol Wuj. This is the way of the Popol Wuj that show how the ancestors created harmony and peace to bring about the balance in nature to cause their crops to flower and fruit with wealth and prosperity. This is really the backdrop of the Popol Wuj as it takes us along on a transformative journey on  paths of initiation and sacrifice that we will take with Hero Twins and Ancestral Mothers and Fathers find themselves on their initiatory paths of tests and trials that show them who they are on their paths of ordeal on the Face of the Earth. The Popol Wuj is a powerful Indigenous Myth that originates long before any European influence on its ancestral narrative that is written in the original Maya Kʼicheʼ language that speaks to us in authentic ways that call for its mythic images and metaphorical words to be translated in ways that reflect the the Kʼicheʼ World as it experienced in the context of the Natural Kʼicheʼ World and the Cultural Context of the Kʼicheʼ People; Kʼicheʼ People. It is this Natural World and Cultural Context in which the Popol Wuj is enveloped as a Sacred Bundle of Mythic Metaphor and Cultural Significations that this Translation and Interpretation is grounded in order that the reader experience the original meaning of the Popol Wuj as close as possible to the way it was once understood by the Nobles and Vassals of the Kʼicheʼ Kingdom. body: I think of the Popol Wuj in this way now that I know it in the profound way a Translator and Interpreter of a Peopleʼs Sacred History comes to know an Ancient Ancestral Account of a People; of a Pueblo; the Kʼicheʼ Maya in the case of the Popol Wuj. These People who are a Pueblo who are formed and shaped by the metaphors that are formed and shaped in the sacred narratives told in the Popol Wuj. The Kʼicheʼ Maya continue to live by the ways of life found in the Popol Wuj even though they no longer read its word or act it out as ritual drama the way it once was acted out long ago. The Kʼicheʼ Maya were formed and shaped by the words and images; metaphors and mythic imagination of the Popol Wuj that once  molded and modeled them into a People; a Pueblo so that now the Popol Wuj continues to form and shape  the deep structure that forms and shapes their lives without anyone ever really reading it anymore. But that is changing and changing fast which one of the many reasons I decide to go back to work Translating and Interpreting its mythopoetic voice so that English speaking descendants of the Maya and Mesoamericans as well as all of their contemporaries could enjoy a translation that reflected the original words and metaphors of the Popol Wuj all which is nested in the natural world and cultural space the Popol Wuj originates as the Ancient Ancestral Account of the Kʼicheʼ People that tells the story of all they did as Kʼicheʼ People that lived together as the Kʼicheʼ Pueblo. Those are the stories told in the Popol Wuj; stories that are what one might call stories that reflect mythic archetypes in spectacularly archetypal ways in which you will recognize these mythic archetype as part of your collective unconsciousness as if you had already read them somewhere before.

body: In this sense the Popol Wuj is a ʼperfectʼ myth of an Indigenous People that makes one feel right at home in their world where the sense of belonging is felt page after page. Maya myth is horticultural myth where the Grandmother is Matriarch who transforms into a Jaguar in the Middle of the Night to ruin the work of grandsons who try to deceive here in the Middle of the Day. It takes a great deal of interpretation now-a-days since most of us have unintentionally been trained by empirical-rational-analytical forms of education to be literal minded beings who need someone to connect the dots. Popol Wuj asks us to use our imagination to ʼmake believeʼ and this is why the Interpreter is here next to the Translator to assist the reader in their reading of myth in a world in which reading myth takes a lot more realizing that once upon a time the storyteller didnʼt have to say Grandmother transformed into all the animals, not just one. She could be a Morning Dove and then Coati and now the Jaguar on her mountain throne dreaming up the wives of the men she just formed and shaped out of ground corn dough. This has been my work now for forty years; working with this mythic history that is the sacred history known as the Popol Wuj.

body: I began my study long ago when my father was killed and just disappeared in a blazing ball of fire in an industrial accident. Then when I read the Popol Wuj I could see this is what happened to the Hero Twins of the Popol Wuj; their father was nowhere to be found, his soul and spirit were out their but his face was nowhere to be seen anymore. Not only that but it was the story that the little Maya boys living around the house lived out in lives that had been turned into a nightmare by both the military and guerrilla. The only reading that made real sense was reading the Popol Wuj first in English then in Kʼicheʼ until one day I began translating for myself. Just like that I found the myth I would live by the rest of my life. This is that myth; this is that book, the Book of Council known as the Popol Wuj. Myth teaches us transcendent truths about death and rebirth while teaching us about the meaning and purpose of life. Good luck living as a human being on the Face of the Earth without a myth; good luck with that because a human being without a myth to live by is a human being without a mythic map of meaning that helps them find their way and that is just no good; no good at all. That is why I dedicated my life to translating and interpreting this sacred myth; this mythic history; this sacred history that is this Maya Myth of Maize. I have been working on it because of the power it has to provide meaning in our lives while showing the way human beings find purpose in life.

body: If one is not interested in reading the Popol Wuj on that level archetypal psychology then there is absolutely nothing that compares for the way the Popol Wuj teaches us about the Maya-Mesoamerican Way of Life. The Popol Wuj teaches us about Mesoamerica in the most detailed way through the language it uses; the archetypal stories of the Maize Deities that it tells; the vast amount of Archaeoastronomy found throughout its constant mirroring of above and below; the archetypal mythic figures of Mesoamerican deities and their archetypal acts performed as expressions of Maya-Mesoamerican myth; in short everything that exists in Maya Culture and Mesoamerican Civilization can be found at one level or another in the Popol Wuj. Popol Wuj is the Rosetta Stone for understanding everything that happens in the Mesoamerican world. It might take a bit of translation, hermeneutics, and interpretive untangling of knots but the Popol Wuj really does tell the story of Mesoamerica from the Cave of Emergence to the Arrival at the Coming Out Place of the Sun there at the Great Temple of Tula-Tollan.

body:
This is why the pages of Interpretation in this Translation are so extensive because of my training as a Historian of Religion and Mesoamericanist. After all, the Popol Wuj takes us through one entire calendar round of the Sacred Calendar and its three hundred days of Eighteen Months of Twenty from the beginning of one growing season to the last five days of the year. It even says as much in its own secret sort of sacred scribal sort of way but it is there for those with eyes to see and an hermeneutical drive to interpret this religion, language, myth, and culture the way it calls us to interpret it. The Popol Wuj begins with the Sowing and Dawning of the New Year on the First Page and ends with a beautiful prayer of petition on the last Five Days of the Wayebʼ right before the beginning of the New Year when Venus is invoke along with the Mam known as the Year-bearer in order to announce the beginning of the New-Year so the Year-Bearer can pick-up his Sacred Bundle from Tollan Tzuy-Wa from Lord Quetzalcoatl to begin making his way walking the Face of the Earth on the Sacred Path of the Sun. This is the story of the Maya as well of Mesoamerican but it isnʼt revealed to the very end.

We are enchanted by the Popol Wuj because the more one understands it as a Mesoamerican text; the more it reveals about Mesoamerica as secret sort of sacred text of Mesoamerica. It literally talks to about Ancient Primordial City known as Teotihuacan spoken of as the First Tula-Tollan which the Primordial Place Emergence out of the Reeds and Rushes known as Pu. Popol Wuj speaks to us about the Divinatory Calendars and their cycles of times as well as the events that occur in divinatory-cyclical-repetitive time and divinations of those events that are repeated in cyclical time.

body:
Popol Wuj is the great Mesoamerican Mythic Masterpiece of the Maize People written by Maya Scribe but in many ways it talks to all Indigenous American People who lived as one with Maize and the eternal lifecycle of Maize. Maize who needs human beings to separate its seeds like tiny skulls of the ancestors taken from the mazorca-head of maize that is like a skull-wrack of well ordered skulls. Each one of the seeds must be taken off as a little skull without a jaw to be taken up in oneʼs hand to be sown  as the seed of ancestor that gives birth as the sprouting forth of the descendant.  These are the metaphorical stories found in the Popol Wuj that show the way of how human beings and the milpa are one and how they need one another to provide and sustain one-an-other.

Popol Wuj tells of the way the Maize People confront life, death and rebirth as the Cane of Maize both known as Aj or Cane in which the Divine Ancestors seek to be replaced by their Descendants just as their Descendants seek to become exact replicas and replacements of their powerful transforming ancestors known as Nawales in stories that transform into other stories. This story of the transforming Maize Beings transforms into the stories of the Divine Ancestors becoming Nawales; and, those Nawales transforming the Sky-Earth using their magical transforming ancestral power with their capability and capacity to become whatever they needed to become to bring about prosperity and abundance in a naturally bountiful world: rain, wind, fog, dew, lightning, thunder, bees, and hummingbirds. This is the bountiful world in which the Popol Wuj teaches its People; Pueblo they must never give up on trying to make the impossible possible in order to accomplish those acts of self-sacrifice and remembrance that bring about harmony and balance in life lived out on the Face of the Earth.  Popol Wuj then above all that teaches all that come to it to sacrifice themselves to something much bigger than themselves without ever making a big deal of oneself through self-aggrandizement. The worst sin of all in the Maya world in which humility and self-effacement with pride is the golden path to the good life.

body: Popol Wuj is the story of the Hero Twins who are coaxed into taking up the road to Xibʼalbʼaʼ to look for the face of their dead Fathers by descending down into the Underworld to confront the Lords of Death; Lords of Disease. After endless confrontations with Death and surviving one test after the next to survive one ordeal after the next to overcome one trial after the next they finally defeat the Lords of Death to then find their dead Father bones buried beside the Ballcourt where they have been playing ball all along on the Sacrificial Ballcourt of Sacrifice. This then is when they are finally able to ʼrememberʼ their Fathers to then perform the ritual adornment-ʼkaweqaʼ to ʼadornʼ their ʼbonesʼ to console their Fathersʼ ʼheartsʼ and comfort their Fathersʼ ʼsoulsʼ so the Boys, the Sons, the  Twins can move on in their lives now that have brought order and harmony to the ʼbonesʼ of their Fathers. The bones that will become the maize seed of the next Sun, the next Age, the next Era of the Maize People and their Sun. Now they can bring to fulfillment that ʼwhich is theirsʼ to fruition; now they can take up the road of their destiny that only they can bring to fruition.  The Popol Wuj is a profound mythological narrative that one can go deeper into without every reaching the very bottom of the endless possibilities of interpretation and understanding found within its mythic imagination and the imaginal realm that is formed and shaped from its mythical metaphors and archetypal images.

source: Popol Wuj: Introduction (Translation and Interpretation), Vincent James Stanzione, February 2024
body: The Popol Wuj is known as Ojer Tzij; Ancient Word, Ancestral Story to the Scribal Lords of the Kʼicheʼ Maya who wrote this Book of Council spoken of as Popol Wuj. There once were many Council Books of the Noble Lords that were known as the Books of Council; all of them known as Popol Wuj. Only one of these Books of Council exists today so we have come to call it ʼtheʼ Popol Wuj that is ʼtheʼ Council Book of the Noble Lords of Kʼicheʼ that was also the Book of the People; Book of the Pueblo; Book of the Commons: Popol Wuj. The Popol Wuj teaches the Noble Lords how to treat their Vassals and Subjects with respect by treating them as Precious Daughters; Precious Sons: Saqil Al; Saqil Kʼajol; Divine Daughters; Sacred Sons. The sacred stories of the Popol Wuj form and shape the Kʼicheʼ People by showing them how to act and speak as the Divine Ancestors spoke and acted. The ancestral narratives of the Popol Wuj mold and model the Noble Lords and Vassals by showing how not to act; how not to speak. But because we only have one Popol Wuj to learn from we can take a moment to realize this is it; this is ʼtheʼ Book of Council; this is ʼtheʼ Popol Wuj so if we want to learn those transcendent truths that can always be learned from mythic narratives then there is nothing like the Popol Wuj to learn those transcendent truths that come from transcendent beauty that manifests as the transcendent good of a people who live in peace and harmony with one another known in the Popol Wuj as Saq Amaqʼ and Saq Kʼaslem; Precious, Perfect Pueblo; Precious, Perfect Life; Sacred Pueblo; Sacred Life. This ethical beauty calls forth a transcendent truth about life on Earth spoke of here in the Popol Wuj as the perfect reciprocity between all the actors and agents that play their role in this epic myth of the Maya.

body: The Popol Wuj tells of how the Kabʼawil or Divinities provide and sustain the Maize in the Milpa with clouds and rain; sun and warmth; the Pueblo of Vassals and Subjects provide and sustain the Kabʼawil who provide the Vassals and Subjects with their Maize and Milpa through the warmth and rain; sun and clouds; the Noble Lords Provide the People with their Kʼabʼawil while giving sacrifice to their Kabʼawil to guide and protect their Vassals and Subjects; the Kabʼawil provide and sustain the Noble Lords with guidance and protection so the Noble Lords know what to do next to bring their Pueblo to fruition by bring the Puebloʼs Milpa to fruition; the Milpa comes to fruition to provide and sustain the Pueblo of Vassals and Subjects with their sacred sustenance; to then give themselves up in sacrifice as the Vassals and Subjects who are sacrificed by the Noble Lords who are the Sacrificial Priests who sacrifice their Divine Daughters, Sacred Sons up in sacrifice to the Kabʼawil who are those who transform the Sky-Earth to bring about great abundance to provide and sustain for their People, their Pueblo who they guide and protect through the Noble Lords who are told what to do by the Kabʼawil… And so goes the story of the Providers and the Sustainers in the Popol Wuj known as Tzuqul, Kʼool.

body:
This is where I want to grab your attention and hold it tight because we only have ʼjust one-xa junʼ Popol Wuj and because we only have ʼjust one-xa junʼ Book of Council we must apply ourselves complete to our understanding of it through this translation and interpretation of its words and images. I dislike putting pressure on my reader but we need to make a great deal of effort to ʼdecolonizeʼ our minds and their ways of think there is no sacred text of Indigenous American that we can learn from. That is not true. It is true many Books of Council were burnt but this one was not because it was written specifically as a remembrance of the Ancestral Past and all that the Kʼicheʼ Maya did there that the Noble Lords wanted to be remembered forever. And so we have that written work. This is it written in Translation and Interpreted so it can be better understood in its own cultural context.

It is because we have ʼjust one; xa junʼ Council Book of the Council House of the Noble Lords of the Kʼiche Maya that we are obliged by our own cultural ethics and its historical conscious of the devastation of Indigenous Culture in the America with common cultural consciousnessʼs aspirations to develop our cultural diversity through sacred writing written with sacred language that we must find a way to ʼenter the wordʼ of the Popol Wuj. This wanting to know the ways of Indigenous People is no longer an option because we have entered the period of decolonization in which we are obliged to open our eyes and minds to know the Indigenous People who are here amongst us and have always been here amongst us. We must stop pretending people like the Maya are not the Descendants of a Highly Sophisticated Civilization with extraordinarily refined writing. Here it is in this one last Popol Wuj.

body:
Because here is the thing; just because we have only one Sacred History of all the thousands of the Indigenous People from Ancient America that does not mean that this edition of the Book of Council is somehow ʼjustʼ a left-over or something inferior. Nothing could be more mistaken to think of the Popol Wuj like that. The way we must approach our reading of this Translation and Interpretation of the Ancient Word of the Popol Wuj is to understand it as the most refined work of literature of the Kʼicheʼ Maya Noble Scribes that could have been written because it was written by a committee of specialize chosen Scribes from the Noble Lineages of the Kʼicheʼ Maya. The work of Gary Sparks teach us this and much more about the authors and writing of the Popol Wuj so if you are interest look to Professor Sparks and read his work regarding this truth. Because what he says and what his writing suggests is that during the years of 1554-1555-1556-1557-1558 the Scribes known as the Nim Chʼokoj Ajaw gather together to ʼcelebrateʼ counsel in council as the ʼGivers of Life as the Mothers of the Word; Fathers of the Word who were said to be of unique nature; one of a kind character and essence that brought forth the Ancient Word; Ojer Tzij of the Popol Wuj.

The Popol Wuj is written one generation after the brutal conquest and subjugation of the Kʼicheʼ Maya. This is after the plague has decimated the population and the Conquistadores have enslaved the Maya taking them to the mines in Mexico and Peru or to wash gold in Peru and Colombia. This is a moment in time when the Dominicans have control of the Kʼicheʼ Maya Nobles who they have trained and are training them while writing the Popol Wuj to write in the Latinate Alphabet. The Kʼicheʼ Maya Scribe respond by writing a precious document that is formed and shaped with a mythopoetic language that is as beautiful as it is elegant and sophisticate in it use of a sacred form of Maya Kʼicheʼ.

body: So please approach the Popol Wuj as a Mythic Masterpiece of the Maize People who are also the Kʼicheʼ People of the Kʼicheʼ Pueblo. This is the manifestation of a very High Civilization that has been given the opportunity to express itself using this new alphabet that is transcribing the First Book with their Ancient Writing and the Ilbʼal or Mythic Mapas or Lienzo that all Pueblo once used to teach its youth about their Ancestral Realm and that Realms Ancestral Past. This is what the Popol Wuj is. It the Ancestral Story of  ʼCreation and Destructionʼ of the Ages or Suns known as the ʼForming and Shapingʼ of the Sky-Earth with separation of the Sky from the Water; Water from the Earth to then tell of the ʼForming and Shapingʼ of the Face of the Earth with the Pine Groves, Cypress Groves; Streams and Rivers; the Trees and Vine; Serpents and Snakes; Deer and Birds; Jaguar and Puma; Big Animals, Small Animals; to then tell of the Creation and Destruction of the Ages of the Animal People; the Clay People; Wooden People. At which point this Sacred Scripture of the Kʼicheʼ Maya tells the Hero Twins Stories of the Cultural Heroes Junajpu; Ixbʼalamkej with their Ordering of the Face of the Earth to prepare it for the ʼForming and the Shapingʼ of the People of Maize; Ixim Winaq; Maize People. The Hero Twins must defeat and destroy the Lords of the Death after having destroyed the Arrogant Ones known as the Principal Bird Deity Seven Macaw; Wuqubʼ Kaqix and his Sons Volcano Boy, Sipakna and Earthquake Boy Kabʼraqan after telling the tale of the Four Hundred Boys. These sections of the Blowgun Boy; Junajpu and his twin Little Jaguar-Deer; Ixbʼalamkej are exciting to read and I have done my best to bring them across exactly as they are written in Kʼicheʼ.

body:
At this point the Boys Ascend into the Sky or Ascend into Heaven as the Moon of the Night Sky and the Sun of the Daytime Sky. Now the story of the finding of the sacred substance that will be the essence of the flesh of the Maize Beings is sought out and found so the Grandmother and Matriarch of the Maize People can form and shape the Maize People who will become the First Four Fathers of the Kʼicheʼ Winaq; Kʼicheʼ Amaqʼ who are the Kʼicheʼ People; Kʼicheʼ Pueblo. This story then reveals a story that was told throughout Mesoamerica that is the story of the Dawn of the Sun of the Age of the Pueblo and People one came from. In this case we are told the story of the watching and waiting for the Sun and Age of the Kʼiche Maya and their Era of the Kʼicheʼ People who have their story told of conquest and settlement of the Highlands and Lowlands of Guatemala. What is fascinating is that the stories told of the Kʼicheʼ People and their Sun reflect the Mythic Narratives of the Hero Twins and their lives as Sacred Twins.

The Popol Wuj is a Sacred History that is an integrated Mythic History that teaches us so much about human consciousness and in particular the integral consciousness of the Kʼicheʼ Maya. The Kʼicheʼ were able to integrate their history and their myth through their calendar and its cycles of time to form and shape a very integrated sense of time and its repetition of events in time and space.  So there you have a quick overview of what goes on in the Popol Wuj as it moves as a mythic narrative that reveals itself as a historical narrative where history plays out in mythical ways and myth is told ʼas ifʼ it were the mythic history of the Maize People.

I think that is more than enough to get you oriented towards the secret sort of sacred writing that goes on a ʼplotʼ in the Popol Wuj. So let review just exactly what the Popol Wuj was with regard to the Noble Lords known as Ajaw and the Council House; Popol Ja from which they ruled and the Sacred Reed Mats; Pop that symbolized the power to rule and the origins of the reeds from which originated the Noble Rule and Authority of the Noble Lords which was the Ancient Ancestral Place known as Tollan-Tula and Pu: Pu being the Ancient Reeds and Rushes but also the Great Mesoamerican City known as Teotihuacan: Pu. Let us go back to the Council House of Kʼicheʼ Lords and Nobles and their library where they keep their Ancestorsʼ Memory in Books that are known as Popol Wuj or Book of the Council House or just Book of Council; Council Book.

Before the Spanish Conquest and Invasion of Mesoamerica there were many different Books of Council in the Libraries in the Council Houses of the Noble Lords. These Books of Council of the Popol Ja; Council House existed as Popol Wuj; Council Books were filled with illustrations and writing that told the Pictorial Histories of the Kʼicheʼ Maya People that were their Puebloʼs Ancestral Histories. These Pictorial Histories written and illustrated in ʼscreen-foldʼ books told the Mythic Histories of the Pueblos; they spoke of the Divine Ancestors and Divinities known as the Kabʼawil. Professor Elizabeth Hill Boone has written extensively on these Books that reveal the Sacred Count of the Suns, the Moons, Venus, and the Years that are Pictographic Histories written  in red and black ink telling of the cycles of time and meaning of time. Professor Davíd L. Carrasco and colleague Scott Sessions edited a book titled Cave, City, and Eagleʼs Nest: An Interpretive Journey through the Mapa de Cuauhtinchan No. 2 that tells of a great big Mapa or Lienzo known to the Kʼicheʼ Maya as an Ilbʼal that is an Image to See meaning it is a Mythic Map of Meaning that tells the story of the People of Cuauhtinchan near Puebla Mexico. The Kʼicheʼ Maya Scribes of the Popol Wuj tell us how they lament no longer having in their possession this ʼIlbʼalʼ of theirs with which to write their Peopleʼs Ancestral Story;  Ojer Tzij in this Sacred Ancestral Book known as the Council Book: Popol Wuj.

This Translation and Interpretation of the Popol Wuj written here comes as an extension of my being invited to participate on the Mapa de Cuauhtinchan Project at Harvard University with Prof. Carrasco and his team of scholars who came together to work on deciphering the Mapa. What one learned there amongst many other important ideas from Mesoamerica is that the Pueblos of Mesoamerica illustrated and painted Pictorial Histories upon which their youth learned about their ʼterritory-chinamitʼ to then sing its songs and dance its dances when it came time to be initiated into the Pueblo-Amaqʼ as a member of the People-Winaqʼ and this is exactly what is going on here with this precious Book of Council that tell the Ancestral History of the Kʼicheʼ Lineages known today as the Maya. The Ojer Tzij; Ancient Word of the Ancestral Story tells the entire History of the Kʼicheʼ Maya People in the Maya Kʼicheʼ Language in the most aesthetically pleasing sacred language one can imagine. This is why I have included a great deal of the original Maya Kʼicheʼ language so the reader can learn to name the names of the divinities, divine ancestors, mythic figures, mythic heroes and rivals, noble lords, places, and things that are found here in this Translation and Interpretation of the Popol Wuj.

The Popol Wuj translated here come from the work of Noble Kʼicheʼ Maya Scribes who are transcribing their Divine Ancestors First Books; Ancient Books known as Nabʼe  Wujil with their Ojer Tzibʼam Ancient Writing; Ancestral Script. The Noble Scribes of the Kʼiche known as the Nim Chʼokoj Ajaw or Great Lords of the Mico de León were specialist from the Three Principal Lineages of the Kʼicheʼ: Kaweq, Nijaʼibʼabʼ, and Ajaw Kʼicheʼ Lineages translated as the Kaweq; the Adorned Ones; the Great House; Lord Kʼicheʼ lineage. The translation of the Kaweq as the Adorned Ones comes from a popular translation that I like because it comes from an Elderly Day-Keeper from Kʼicheʼ explained to be in the Ancient City of the Kʼicheʼ of Qʼumaraq Aaj. I mention it here because this translation is a translation that does rely heavily on academics and scholars yet when their work has remained indecisive I brought my questions with my Kʼicheʼ edition of the Popol Wuj by Luis Enrique Sam Colop to Qʼumaraq Aaj to consult the Kʼicheʼ Maya themselves. Academics, especially linguists, are not so much in favor of this popular ethnographic work but as a foreigner-kaxlan who now lives with the Maya for thirty-five years I know it is the ʼdecolonizedʼ direction that I feel is more than justified. I like this interpretation of the Kaweq as being the ʼAdorned Onesʼ because they were the Noble Lords of the Kʼicheʼ who were the most adorned and wrote about adorned rulers in the Popol Wuj in very significant ways. Kaweq are the most powerful lineage of the Kʼicheʼ and thus must have been well adorned as this Book of Council will most definitely attest!

The Kʼicheʼ Maya Scribes who name themselves at the end of their Popol Wuj as the Nim Chʼokoj Ajaw who are the Mother-Fathers of the Word; Chuch Tzij-Qajaw Tzij who are the one and only givers of life of the Ancient Word of the Pueblo Kʼicheʼ who were of a very special nature that had gathered together in council as Masters of the Word to write the Ancestral History of the Kʼicheʼ Winaq; Kʼicheʼ Amaqʼ there was no longer the Ilbʼal the Place to See their Pictorial History because that which was once was of the Noble Lords no could be found for it was lost. And with that statement the scribes say so ends our telling of all that was done by those who are they of the Kʼicheʼ now known as Santa Cruz.

body: Because those Books of Council; Popol Wuj and Mapa of Meaning; Ilbʼal were burnt in great fires set by Franciscan and Dominican Padres all across Mesoamerica we now have very  few Books of Council. But we do have this Book of Council. We do have this Popol Wuj with its Old Way of Speaking to us across these last five centuries. It was exactly five hundred years ago that the Castilians burnt Qʼumaraq Aaj on the March 7th, 1524 on the quintessential day of sacrificial fire known as Kajibʼ Kʼat-Four Net; Four Fire; Four Day of Ceremonial Fire; Kʼat Harvest Net; Kʼat the Last Lords of the Kaweq Lineage of the Kʼicheʼ Maya were burnt to death in a great sacrificial fire. Nine Dog; Bʼelejebʼ Tzʼiʼ Three Deer; Oxibʼ Kej were burnt to death by Pedro de Alvarado known as the New Sun el Adelantado de los Conquistadores.  Yet if these deaths are read as the deaths of the Hero Twins, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej, and if one knows the significance of these names with regard to the divinations and prognostications of the Sacred Count of the Day then what seems like a complete dynastic disaster becomes the announcement of the Kʼicheʼ taking back their territory and gaining rulership once again. This is what is happening today and why translating and interpreting the Popol Wuj at this time amongst the Maya became an empowering experience.  This is why the extent Popol Wuj translated here  is so very precious and deserves our complete attention and best effort to bring out in ways that reflect the Maya Sky-Earth instead of perspectives coming from the outside so that is understood ʼeasierʼ be a foreign audience.

I studied all the linguistic and literal translations of the Popol Wuj that exist today to realize that they did not reflect the cultural and religious nuance of the Kʼicheʼ Maya to then go back to work staying close to the metaphors and mythical sense of the original writing of the Ojer Tzij until I was able to accomplish a translation that complete different from past English Translation by bring forth a replica of Ancient Word; Ojer Tzij in English. This is why I am writing you an Introduction to this Translation and Interpretation so you will be able to enter the Ojer Tzij; Ancient Word of the Kʼicheʼ Maya with a great deal of confidence due to the cultural orientation provided for you in order to sustain the mythic metaphors of the Popol Wuj through the knowledge provided as a form of sacred sustenance by preparing the reader through a familiarization with the primary metaphors and names explained to you here in this Introduction to the Translation and Interpretation of the Popol Wuj.

All of this information is found in the Translation and Interpretation so if you would rather skip ahead to the English Translation then by all means do so because in the end everything you will find in this introduction is found in the main text. You will learn a great deal about the Kʼicheʼ Maya in this Introduction but some people prefer to go right into their reading of Popol Wuj of the Kʼicheʼ Maya.  The Popol Wuj that  is the Kʼicheʼ Mayaʼs Ancestral History that states in the first lines that is the Ancient Word; Ojer Tzij that tells of ʼeverythingʼ that was done by the Kʼicheʼ People; Kʼicheʼ Pueblo in the Place known as Kʼicheʼ. Popol Wuj then might be best thought of as the Sacred Book of the Kʼicheʼ Maya People and their Pueblo known today as it was always known: Kʼicheʼ.

These two voices are: one, the voice of translation; and, two, the voice of interpretation and alternative translation. This English Translation of the Popol Wuj is the primary narrative voice while the English Interpretation of the Popol Wuj is the secondary narrative voice. The two narrative voices twinning one another by interpretive voice complementing and collaborating with the translated text of the Popol Wuj in order provide greater understanding and sustain its cultural meaning with additional cultural and historical context.

This English Translation-Interpretation of the Popol Wuj calls for two different yet similar looking texts within one larger singular text and this is because of the twin character of the text where the English Translation is the Principal Text that acts as  the ʼPersona or Faceʼ of this ʼtwinʼ text that is complemented by the English Interpretation that supports the primary text of interpretation by acting as a companion interpretive text that provides support for the primary text of the English Translation of the Popol Wuj. This secondary interpretive text is best read as a complementary sort of twin text to the translation that as a twinning interpretive text has a more cooperative and collaborative quality as the interpretive aspect of this translation and interpretation of the Popol Wuj; a translation and interpretation of the Popol Wuj found in one single book formed and shaped by two twin texts that run together as the primary English Translation of the Popol Wuj and its twin, the complementary and collaborative interpretation that are written to be easily distinguished from one another by using two different size fonts.

Since the English Translation and English Interpretation are written in different narrative voices I realized that as the author of  both voices I needed to make a distinction so that the translation remained true to the original Maya Kʼicheʼ language. I had to separate translation from interpretation to remain true to the Maya Kʼicheʼ Popol Wuj in order to translate its mythic words and mythic metaphors with the highest regard and deepest respect by using two separate voices. By implementing these two different voices I was able to maintain the boundaries between the pure translation of the original Popol Wuj and the complementary more collaborative quality of the interpretation with its interpretive voice in order to not over interpret the original text. By keeping the two twin-like texts separate from one another the interpretive text is able to play its role as a complementary kind of collaborative cultural contextualization of the primary English Translation the embodies and reflects the original Maya Kʼicheʼ Language Popol Wuj without that text of translation being overwhelmed by interpretation and explanation coming from studies of the Maya and Mesoamerica language and culture inside the mythopoetic text.
